title: America's Top Trade Negotiator Will Fly to India the Week After G7. A Deal, Officials Say, Is Possible.
excerpt: USTR Jamieson Greer's visit follows months of back-and-forth on tariffs, Section 301 probes, and a bilateral framework that could reshape how NRIs send goods — and money — across both countries.
body:
The man who will decide whether American tariffs on Indian goods stay at 18 per cent or climb higher is booking a flight to New Delhi.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will travel to India the week after the G7 summit in Evian, a senior U.S. administration official confirmed on Saturday. The official described a trade agreement as "possible" — the most optimistic language Washington has used since the bilateral framework was announced in February.

The visit means India will host America's chief trade negotiator twice in six weeks. Greer's team was last in New Delhi in early June, when Indian and American officials worked through tariff schedules, agricultural market access, and non-tariff barriers across multiple sectors.

## The G7 Sets the Table

Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump are expected to hold bilateral talks at the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, between June 15 and 17. Trade will dominate the conversation, but the official was clear: no deal will be signed at the summit itself. The heavy lifting comes after, when Greer's delegation lands in India.

The meeting will be the first face-to-face between Modi and Trump since India's brief conflict with Pakistan last year — a subject that strained ties after Trump repeatedly claimed, and India denied, that he personally intervened to end the hostilities.

Recent high-level visits have helped ease the friction. Secretary of State Marco Rubio travelled to India last month and covered trade, visas, maritime security, and the Middle East in a single trip. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum earlier this month that he was "very optimistic" about closing a deal.

## What Is Actually on the Table

The February framework established broad strokes: the U.S. would reduce tariffs on most Indian goods to 18 per cent from 50 per cent, while India committed to lowering duties on American industrial goods to zero and cutting tariffs on tree nuts, wine, spirits, fruits, and vegetables.

India's Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said last week that both sides were "fast moving towards closing all the open ends" and that the first tranche could be executed by mid-July. But two investigations launched by the USTR under Section 301 — one alleging forced labour in Indian supply chains, the other claiming structural overcapacity in textiles and steel — have complicated the timeline.

India has firmly rejected both allegations. At the G7, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Kumar Sinha told reporters that the U.S. had not identified any specific Indian policies or practices to support the overcapacity claim. "India does not have overcapacity in anything," he said.

Washington has also proposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff on imports from India and roughly 60 other countries on forced-labour grounds. India says the charges are not final and is engaging through the Section 301 process.

## The H-1B Factor

Visas will also be on the agenda. The $100,000 H-1B fee that Trump imposed last September was struck down by a federal judge on June 8, and a Republican congressman has already introduced legislation — the PROTECT Act — to codify the fee through Congress. Any trade conversation between Modi and Trump will inevitably touch the visa pipeline that fuels India's single largest export to the United States: skilled labour.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly 4.5 million Indian Americans and millions more with business ties spanning both countries, the stakes are immediate. A successful first tranche would lock in preferential access for Indian exports, lower the cost of American goods entering India, and potentially provide guardrails against future tariff escalation. Failure — or indefinite delay — would leave Indian exporters paying some of the highest tariff rates any major trading partner faces.

The next two weeks will determine whether the February handshake becomes a binding agreement or joins the long list of frameworks that never made it to paper.
